name: SIGMA - Sustained Low-and-Slow SSH Session Cadence [threshold]
description: Elastic threshold companion for rules/sigma/net_zeek_ssh_session_cadence_sustained.yml (issue #392, found during #332's security-auditor review). Alerts when a single source (source.ip) establishes >=15 SSH sessions (event.dataset:zeek.ssh, any client version-exchange banner Zeek parsed) within a 30-minute lookback - a rate of roughly 0.5 sessions/minute, genuinely below both policy/protocols/ssh/detect-bruteforcing's own steady-state rate (30 failed auths/30 minutes, ~1/minute) and the shorter-window net_zeek_ssh_session_cadence.yml companion (5 sessions/10 minutes, the SAME ~1/minute rate - a burst-latency improvement, not a lower rate floor; see that rule's own "HONEST FRAMING" note, which named this exact gap and filed it as a follow-up rather than closing it there). #332's own review derived the concrete evasion this rule closes: one SSH connection every 2 minutes = 15 sessions/30min, invisible to both prior rules - with OpenSSH's default MaxAuthTries:6, that's up to ~180 guesses/hour sustained indefinitely with zero T1110 signal anywhere in this pipeline. HONEST FRAMING (same discipline as the shorter-window rule): this does NOT close the underlying cat-and-mouse problem, only moves the rate floor lower - an attacker pacing under 15 sessions/30min evades this rule too, at a correspondingly slower guess rate. No per-source threshold, at any value, reaches zero; not chasing this further with a fourth rule. Reads zeek.ssh directly (not the aggregated notice.log path detect-bruteforcing's T1110 tag uses), so neither path double-counts the same document. security-auditor review (#392): the flat +1-minute-overlap convention every OTHER threshold rule in this corpus uses ("from" exceeds "interval" by exactly 1 minute) is mathematically inadequate for THIS rule specifically, not just incomplete like the others. For a burst-shaped attack (the other rules' target), a 1-minute overlap is a reasonable approximation; for THIS rule's target (15 sessions spread across up to 28 minutes, genuinely window-width-comparable to the 30-minute lookback), the containment band shrinks to (lookback - span) = 3 minutes out of every 30 - a run only fully captures the campaign in a single evaluation ~10% of the time (verified: band-width / interval = 3/30); the other ~90% splits the 15 sessions across two evaluations, neither of which alone crosses threshold.value:15, despite 15 real sessions in under 30 minutes. Fixed, not deferred: "interval": "5m" / "from": "now-35m" (lookback >= interval + the 30-minute detection window, same formula #393 documents for the other two files) guarantees full containment for ANY campaign phase - any 7-minute-or-wider containment band is guaranteed to contain a multiple of a 5-minute interval. Cost: 6 evaluations per 30 minutes instead of 1 (negligible), and worst-case alert latency drops from up to ~60 minutes (30 min to accumulate + up to 30 min to the next run) to ~5 minutes after the 15th session. This rule shipped its own fix directly rather than following the flat +1m convention the rest of the corpus used at the time, since deferral here would have shipped a rule that misses its own stated purpose ~90% of the time. #393 (filed before this file existed) subsequently applied the identical lookback >= interval + window fix to all 7 OTHER threshold files in the corpus (auth-win-bruteforce-failed-logons, auth-win-bruteforce-source-spray, auth-win-explicit-cred-account-sweep, disc-win-domain-group-discovery-repeat, disc-win-nltest-discovery-repeat, disc-win-user-discovery-repeat, net-zeek-ssh-session-cadence) plus generalized tests/detections/test_live_fire.py's ThresholdLiveFireTests to exercise every threshold file instead of one hardcoded path - the aggregation behavior asserted here for THIS file was live-verified manually during #392's own review (both the original 30m/31m containment failure AND the corrected 5m/35m guarantee), and is now also covered by that generalized automated test.
author: Suburban-SOC
false_positives: An admin or automation tool (Ansible, deployment scripts, health checks) establishing many sequential SSH connections to the same host over a longer window.
A jump host or bastion legitimately proxying multiple real users' sessions from one apparent source IP over an extended period.
